title: Credential value in a MIME base64 text part wrapped across encoded lines
summary: A SendGrid-shaped key is the whole body of a MIME text part whose Content-Transfer-Encoding is base64: the key's 69 octets encode to 92 characters, written as a 76-character line and a 16-character line with a CRLF between them. The key is recoverable only by ignoring the line break and Base64-decoding the two fragments together.
rationale: RFC 2045 section 6.8 requires the encoded output to be in lines of no more than 76 characters and requires decoding software to ignore all line breaks, so any value longer than 57 octets is split by a CRLF in its MIME base64 form. The question the single-run Base64 Scenario does not ask is therefore what the encoded range is when the encoded text is interrupted by a separator the standard says to ignore: the secret bytes are the fragments, and the CRLF between them is either inside the range to cover (the encoded text as a whole) or a separator outside it (the fragments only). The two readings differ by two bytes and are both unresolved here. The same reading also depends on the part being identified as base64 by its header (sections 6.1 and 6.2) and on a Base64 decode being run; nothing here says a reader does either. Contrast and boundary fixtures: the same part inside a multipart/mixed message beside an unrelated base64 part of public text (RFC 2046 section 5.1.1: the CRLF before a boundary delimiter belongs to the delimiter, and a boundary parameter is a delimiter, not part content). Out of scope and unresolved: a credential inside a larger decoded body (it needs a decoded sub-range, which the schema does not represent), and nested encodings.

expectation.rationale: RFC 2045 and RFC 2046 define the line wrapping, the decoding and the part structure; neither says anything about confidentiality or about which bytes of an encoded run a reader should cover, so the standards support the mechanism and no outcome. The candidate reading, recorded on the fixtures as non-asserting data, is must-flag with the two Base64 fragments as the secret bytes. It follows the maintainer decision for encoded values (the encoded text is the range) only if the separator bytes are counted as inside that range, and the decision for separator-split values (the fragments are the secret) only if they are not; the records of those decisions do not choose between them for a wrapped MIME body. What would settle it: a maintainer decision naming wrapped Base64 MIME bodies, and a mapping contract with the evaluation consumer for findings on decoded text.

sources.supports: Base64 encoded output must be represented in lines of no more than 76 characters; all line breaks or other characters not found in the Base64 alphabet must be ignored by decoding software.
The Content-Transfer-Encoding value specifies the decoding operation that restores the body to its original form; 7bit is assumed when the field is absent.

A boundary delimiter line is two hyphens followed by the boundary parameter value; the CRLF preceding it is attached to the delimiter, not to the preceding part; boundary delimiters must not appear within the encapsulated material.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed. Authored from RFC 2045 and RFC 2046 read on 2026-10-04, before any scanner was consulted. The expectation is unresolved: the standards give the mechanism, not a confidentiality outcome.
